A major reason why US politics is two party is because of our voting system. First past the post / plurality systems are so broken. Imagine a state here is evenly broken down into 25% democrat, 20% republican, 15% libertarian, 15% green, 10% far far left, 10% far far right, 5% other. If that state has 100 representatives it'd make sense for 25 of them to be democrat, 20 of them to be republican, 15 of them to libertarian, and so on. With our system you get 100 democrat representatives instead.

In first past the post if you have 11% of the vote you get 100% of the representation so long as the #2 candidate only got 10% of the vote. The way we force this system to work, if you can call it working, in states is that we carve the states up into little arbitrary distracts (see: "gerrymandering" for when politicians carve these districts up illicitly for political gains) and each of these districts then votes for a single representative using first past the post. So when the political parties are evenly distributed you end up with 100 elections that go: #1 is democrat with 25, #2 is republican with 20%, etc. And so the democrats end up getting every single seat.

This system destroys the chances of any third party gaining power and inevitably leads to two huge parties. Imagine 4 parties are running for a seat with about equal shares of the vote. Party 1 says to Party 2, "You know.. I know we don't agree on all that much, but if we team up we could share the representation. If we don't, there's a good chance we get 0% of the representation!" Of course parties 3 and 4 see this happening and do the exact same thing. This is why in the US the makeup of the parties is often completely contradictory. Libertarians and christian fundamentalists have next to nothing in common politically speaking, but they vote for the same party. Similarly your average liberal has next to nothing in common with the authoritarian left, but they vote for the same party.
